div.p: Exclusive illustration of E.P. , lyrical poet, presenting Ulixes , wellknown elephant, to the American public. Πόλλα κρόνια !

postscript.p: P.S. This animal has just been decorated (see wreath) by the Stockholm Thickhide Society .

div.note: This postcard was addressed by JJ “all’egregio sig. [to Mr.] Ezra Pound, Hotel Mignon, Rapallo (Italie),” and was redirected in another hand to “Hotel Roma, Siracusa, Sicilia.” After three years in Paris, Pound had begun to feel restless again and was gravitating towards Italy, a country whose beauty and climate he had discovered more than a decade earlier. He and his wife Dorothy, née Shakespear (1886-1973), stayed often in the Hotel Mignon during visits to the coastal town of Rapallo, on the Gulf of Tigullio, some fifteen miles from Genoa. They were at the Hotel Mignon during the early months of 1924, then visited Perugia and Assisi in May before returning to Paris in June. As of October they were back in Rapallo where Pound played tennis, convalesced from appendicitis, read deeply in the writings of American presidents, and worked on his long poem, The Cantos. He and Dorothy were in Taormina, on the island of Sicily, for the Christmas holiday and were established in the Hotel Roma in Siracusa by January 1925, where they were visited by W.B. Yeats and his wife. At each stop, Pound considered the prospects for settling. Taormina was “a bit small for continued residence”; Siracusa “[n]ot exactly habitable”; Palermo not good for “tennis – unless one pays 120 fr. per day at Swynk hotel” (Ezra Pound to His Parents: Letters 1895-1929, ed. Mary de Rachewiltz et al. [Oxford: Oxford University Press, 2010], 550-51). Back in Rapallo in February 1925, they soon found a top-floor apartment at 12 via Marsala, with views of the sea and the hills, perfect for the artist Dorothy who liked to sketch natural scenes and the colors of the sea. Here they remained for nearly twenty years.

The tinted photograph on the face of the postcard shows a young girl in a red dress, white stockings, and Mary Jane shoes, holding a small bunch of flowers and resting her other arm on the tusk of a small elephant whose head is crowned with a cluster of mistletoe. The printed caption at top right reads “Bonne Année” (“Happy New Year”).

JJ often thought of Pound less as an author in his own right than as a useful journalistic champion of A Portrait of the Artist as a Young Man and Ulysses. Around this time, or shortly before, JJ recorded a dream about Leopold and Molly Bloom in which there was a sudden “shout of laughter from some American journalists … led by Ezra Pound” (Ellmann, JJ 549). As in the dream, JJ’s playful gloss of this postcard image hints at his view of Pound as promoter-entertainer, a brash P.T. Barnum displaying his latest discovery, the elephant laureate. As JJ’s art progressed towards the dense verbal experiments of Finnegans Wake, Pound’s interest and sympathy in his work waned, so that by early 1927 JJ could write: “[Pound] understood certain aspects of [Ulysses] very quickly and that was more than enough then. He makes brilliant discoveries and howling blunders” (LI 249).

note.p: “Ulixes” is an alternative Latin form of “Ulysses.” JJ’s message acknowledges Pound’s important role in introducing his masterwork Ulysses to the American public through its serialization in the New York magazine The Little Review, of which Pound was foreign editor from 1917 to 1919.

There is quite possibly another playful allusion here. In 1888, the American writer and journalist Charles Dwight Willard (1860-1914) published a whimsical story called “The Fall of Ulysses” in the San Francisco Argonaut, and the story was widely reprinted in newspapers in America and Britain in the years that followed. The tale was also translated into various languages and circulated in anonymous and misattributed forms. It received renewed exposure when it was published as a book, The Fall of Ulysses: An Elephant Story (New York: George H. Doran Company, 1912). In it, the narrator tells of “the calamity that overtook Ulysses,” a “genuine Asiatic elephant” that has come into his possession and is so intelligent that the narrator is able to teach him to read and write (pages are unnumbered). Ulysses becomes a voracious reader of all manner of books, from novels to philosophical tomes, and grows so scornful of his owner’s intellectual limitations that one day he asks him to explain why their positions of master and servant should not be reversed. The narrator conceives a plan for reasserting his dominance and challenges Ulysses to the “last and severest [test] to which culture and intelligence may be submitted”: the elephant must both “understand and enjoy” Robert Browning’s long narrative poem Sordello (1840), a work that is “a shibboleth by which the true disciples of sweetness and light may distinguish themselves from the miscellaneous herds of Philistines.” Ulysses is so frustrated by his inability to comprehend Sordello that he goes mad and plunges off a rocky bank to his death. The book ends with an author’s note explaining that of all Browning’s works, Sordello “is generally rated the most mysterious and perplexing.”

Sordello, a fictionalized account of a 13th-century Italian troubadour, was a favorite poem of Pound’s. He wrote his father in 1915 that Sordello “takes a bit of reading” but “is a great work & worth the trouble of hacking it out. I began to get it on about the 6th reading. … It is probably the greatest poem in English. Certainly the best long poem in English since Chaucer. You’ll have to read it sometime as my big long endless poem that I am now struggling with, starts off with a barrel full of allusions to ‘Sordello’” (Ezra Pound to His Parents: Letters 1895-1929, 360). “Three Cantos,” Pound’s “long endless” approach to his lifelong epic project, appeared in various forms from 1917 on. It begins: “Hang it all, there can be but one Sordello!” (“Three Cantos. I,” Poetry, vol. 10, no. 3 [June 1917]: 113). Pound goes on to employ many direct and indirect references to Browning’s poem in his effort to give up “th’intaglio method” for a long, capacious art-form that will hold all the thought of “the modern world” (113). For accounts of these early cantos and their relationship to Pound’s epic poem, The Cantos, see JJ to Pound, 30 March 1917, notes; 7 July 1917, notes; 24 July 1917, notes. JJ was aware of “Three Cantos” and told Pound that he wished to read it (JJ to Pound, 9 July 1917).

It is tempting to think that JJ’s humorous postcard glances, via Willard’s tale of Ulysses the overeducated elephant, at the formative roles played by Homer and Browning for Ulysses and The Cantos, respectively.

div.note: JJ’s Greek salutation “πόλλα κρόνια” appears to be a mistake for πόλλα χρόνια, which literally means “many years.” It is easy to employ a kappa (κ) instead of a chi (χ or kh), and JJ’s scrawl may even be a sloppy χ. Our thanks to Stephanie Nelson for assistance with the Greek (for additional details, see JJ to Pound, 6 October 1923, notes).

note.p: JJ refers here to the Nobel Prize in Literature, which had been awarded by the Swedish Royal Academy since 1901 and was conferred annually in a ceremony in Stockholm. W.B. Yeats (1865-1939) had received the prize in 1923, and Pound published an article in the spring of 1924 arguing that “if the award had not gone to Mr Yeats it should have been given to his most distinguished compatriot, the author of ‘ULYSSES’ (“Le Prix Nobel,” Der Querschnitt, vol. 4, no. 1 [Spring 1924]: 41, 43). For more on Pound’s recommendation, see JJ to Pound, 18 July 1924, notes.

In November 1924, the Nobel Prize in Literature was awarded to the Polish writer Wladyslaw Stanislaw Reymont (1867-1925) for his epic novel, The Peasants. The Swedish Academy chose him over Thomas Mann, George Bernard Shaw, and Thomas Hardy.
